summary: An experimental approach for using LDAP as a network information service. It maps information about TCP/IP and UNIX systems, like users, groups and hosts, into directory entries so that they can be looked up through the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2307 defines a way to store user accounts, groups, hosts and other system information in an LDAP directory so multiple computers can look them up from one place.

subtitle: A schema for storing network and system information in LDAP directories

tldr.problem: UNIX systems need to look up users, groups, hosts and services, but flat files and NIS don't scale well. LDAP is flexible but lacks a standard schema for system information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2307 defines LDAP object classes and attributes that map POSIX users, groups, hosts, services, networks and related entities to directory entries. It also specifies how lookups translate to LDAP search filters.
tldr.outcome: The schema became widely adopted as the de facto standard for LDAP-based system administration. RFC 2307 is Experimental, but its classes and attributes remain foundational for LDAP-backed identity and system lookups.

today: RFC 2307 is Experimental, but it became the de facto standard schema for integrating UNIX system information with LDAP. It is widely supported by LDAP servers and by Name Service Switch (NSS) modules on Linux and other systems.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
UNIX systems and TCP/IP networks need to look up many kinds of entities: users, groups, hosts, services, protocols, networks and more. Traditional methods include flat files, NIS and DNS. Each has limitations: flat files don't scale, NIS has limited structure, and DNS is not designed for storing user accounts.

LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) offers a distributed, hierarchical directory with good scalability and extensibility. To use LDAP as a nameservice, there needs to be a schema mapping system entities to LDAP entries. RFC 2307 proposes such a schema.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers need a shared list of who users are and what machines exist. Putting that list in an LDAP directory means everyone can look it up the same way.

sections.title: Object Classes and Attribute Schema
sections.content:
The RFC defines 13 object classes and around 20 new attributes. Key classes include posixAccount (for UNIX user accounts with uid, gid, home directory, shell), shadowAccount (for shadow password fields), posixGroup (for groups), and TCP/IP classes like ipService, ipProtocol, ipHost, ipNetwork, and ipNetmaskNumber.

It also defines two new syntax types: nisNetgroupTripleSyntax for netgroup triples and bootParameterSyntax for boot parameters. Attributes like uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, ipHostNumber and cn capture the necessary information to map to traditional system structures.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of thing - a user, a group, a computer - gets its own type of entry with the right fields. That makes it easy to find exactly what you need.

sections.title: Lookup Methods and Mapping
sections.content:
RFC 2307 maps traditional C library lookups to LDAP search filters. For example, getpwnam('lester') becomes (&(objectClass=posixAccount)(uid=lester)). gethostbyname('host.example.com') becomes (&(objectClass=ipHost)(cn=host.example.com)).

A Directory User Agent (DUA) such as an LDAP-aware library or an LDAP-to-NIS gateway performs these searches. For entities with multiple aliases, the canonical name is typically the RDN, and other values are aliases. Passwords in userPassword should be tagged by scheme (e.g. {crypt}...), and the DUA should use the first scheme it understands.
sections.plainLanguage: When a program looks someone up by name, it just asks the directory for an account with that login name. The directory returns the matching record.

sections.title: Advanced Features
sections.content:
ShadowAccount lets password aging and expiration be stored separately from the encrypted password, supporting password policies while restricting access to sensitive data. nisNetgroup represents NIS-style netgroups as directory entries.

ipService can represent multiple (port, protocol) pairs in one entry. bootableDevice and ieee802Device support network boot and MAC address storage. These allow the schema to cover a broad range of system administration needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema goes beyond users and hosts - it can also handle password expiry rules, netgroups, network services, and boot info.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Access control is critical. Sensitive attributes (especially password hashes) must be protected. The RFC recommends discretionary access control, limiting who can read or modify entries. Users should typically only be able to change their own passwords.

Only administrators should modify sensitive fields like uidNumber and gidNumber, since changing them can affect system security. For gateways republishing data, the subtree should be in the same administrative domain. The RFC notes crypt passwords are vulnerable to dictionary attacks, so strong security environments may need additional protections or dedicated authentication services.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to be careful about permissions. Only admins should change ID numbers, and password data must be well protected.
